title: The Great Wall of China is visible from space.
description:
The Great Wall of China is visible from space. It's repeated so often it feels like common knowledge. It has never been true, and how the claim got started is stranger than the myth itself.

It comes from a 1932 Ripley's Believe It or Not cartoon. Nobody had been to space yet. The claim wasn't a report of what someone saw, it was a guess, printed as fact, decades before Yuri Gagarin's first orbital flight in 1961.

China's first astronaut. After 14 orbits aboard Shenzhou 5, he came back down and told reporters the scenery was beautiful, but he hadn't seen the Great Wall. China's own education ministry then corrected a textbook that had taught the myth as fact.

Apollo's Neil Armstrong said no human structures are visible from the Moon. Shuttle astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman put it plainly: he never saw the Great Wall. From low orbit, under near-perfect light, the wall is sometimes barely visible, and easily mistaken for an ordinary road.

Roughly how wide the wall is. A structure can stretch for thousands of kilometres and still be invisible from orbit if it's no wider than a road, length was never the problem.

Sources:
- https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/great-wall-of-china-from-space/ - read in full 1 Sep 2026 (Mara Hvistendahl, 21 Feb 2008): the myth that the Great Wall is visible from space predates spaceflight, tracing to a 1932 Ripley's Believe It or Not cartoon, three decades before Yuri Gagarin's first orbital flight; Apollo astronauts including Neil Armstrong stated no human structures are visible from the Moon; NASA oral histories quote Shuttle astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman saying he never saw the Great Wall from orbit; NASA's own published assessment is that the wall is barely visible even from 180 miles up and is comparable in width to a highway.
- https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2003/10/17/chinas-spaceman-shatters-a-myth - read in full 1 Sep 2026: contemporaneous report on Yang Liwei, China's first astronaut, completing 14 orbits aboard Shenzhou 5 in October 2003 and telling reporters on his return that the scenery was beautiful but he didn't see the Great Wall, directly puncturing the myth for a domestic Chinese audience; reports that China's Ministry of Education subsequently corrected an elementary-school textbook that had stated the wall was visible from space.
